newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief declares self head of state.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief declares self head of state.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Saturday was on the verge of realising a three-decade-old dream: the overthrow of his arch-enemy President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Mobutu, 66, departed from the Zairean capital Kinshasa on Friday after generals said they could not guarantee his security. It was later announced Mobutu was stepping aside after 32 years and had left his emergency-rule government in charge of national policy.
On Saturday, Kabila said he had taken over as head of state with the agreement of army generals in Kinshasa.
Speaking to reporters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi, Kabila said he expected his forces to have complete control of the capital within hours.
Despite international peace mediation, Kabila always seemed intent on entering Kinshasa as a military victor after an eight-month campaign across Africa's third largest country.
He snubbed Mobutu and South Africa President Nelson Mandela by failing even to turn up for a second round of face-to-face talks on a South African navy ship on May 14, citing security reasons.
"The question of a ceasefire is not part of his (Kabila's) vocabulary," Mandela had said after a first round of talks he mediated on May 4.

As his troops headed toward Kinshasa, Kabila's forces met their heaviest resistance at Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) east of the capital. Aid sources said hundreds of people were killed in heavy fighting.
On the humanitarian front, his rebels were condemned over reports they were massacring Rwandan refugees.
They then prevented a U.N. team from investigating.

Kabila, 56, heads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), an alliance of four obscure political groups, formed last October 8 with Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis as the cutting edge of their revolt against Mobutu.

"My long years of struggle were like spreading fertiliser on a field. But now it is time to harvest," the short, burly rebel leader -- who speaks perfect English -- told Reuters recently at his headquarters in southeastern Zaire.
Known by supporters as Mzee, the Swahili word for Grand Old Man, Kabila is not an ethnic Tutsi. But he has forged close links to Tutsis over the years.
Mobutu supporters accused him of being a puppet of the Banyamulenge, who have been denied citizenship, and ethnic brothers in Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.
The level of support the AFDL rebels received from numerous neighbouring countries as their war against Mobutu gained ground fuelled doubts among some over whether Kabila calls all the shots.
Kabila is from mineral-rich Shaba in southern Zaire but has lived for many years among the Banyamulenge in the Mulenge Mountains south of Uvira, from where he plotted the uprising.
War in eastern Zaire began when the Banyamulenge, a community of roughly 400,000, resisted Zairean attempts to expel them to Rwanda, a land which they left up to 200 years ago.
But its roots go deeper and the rebels have a solid spine of veterans who fought with Rwanda's Tutsis after 1990. Rwanda says it backs his rebellion but denies charges it sent troops to help.
Kabila, stocky with a shaved head, is a former comrade-in -arms of the late Argentine-born revolutionary leader Ernesto "Che" Guevara, who fought in eastern Zaire in the early 1960s.
In 1965 Kabila joined a rebellion in the east led by Pierre Mulele, a minister in Patrice Lumumba's government when the former Belgian Congo just avoided breakup after independence.
A biography, "Che Guevara - A Revolutionary Life" by John Lee Anderson, includes sections of Che's unpublished memoir of the debacle in Congo, where he had pinned his hopes on Kabila.
Initially, Che was impresssed by Kabila, Anderson says.

"Kabila understood perfectly that the principal enemy was North American imperialism," Che wrote. Kabila's revolutionary ideas were "clear, concrete and firm." The United States, in particular, remains worried about his stand on free enterprise.
But after weeks in the eastern Congo jungle, Che became disillusioned with Kabila who seemed reluctant to visit the front and instead drove around Dar es Salaam in a Mercedes Benz.

Che wrote that he and his Cuban fighters were dismayed by the Congolese rebels and their Rwandan Tutsi allies. They were undisciplined and often drunk. They disobeyed their officers and deserted in the face of combat.
Mobutu, president since 1965, crushed that rebellion and mercenaries chased Che over a lake into Tanzania.
But Kabila stuck to his mission, and was a regular visitor to Uganda in the late 1980s after Yoweri Museveni's rebels took power.
At the same time, exiled Rwandan Tutsis in top positions in Museveni's army plotted to invade Rwanda. They did so in 1990 and seized power in 1994 after genocide unleashed by Hutu extremists.
Some African states argue Kabila is at the head of a plot to carve out a "Tutsiland" in central Africa. Kabila denies it.
He is married with six children including Joseph, a rebel commander who captured the cities of Kisangani and Lubumbashi.
